extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of classical political philosophy (Plato's Republic)
extracted.subtask_description: Summarize and analyze the types of constitutions and their corresponding character-types as presented in Book VIII of Plato's Republic, including origins, defining features, defects, and transitions between regimes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perfect State: communal institutions for guardians
rubrics_metrics.description: In the perfect State wives and children are to be in common; all education and the pursuits of war and peace are also to be common; rulers/guardians live in common houses and possess no ordinary private property, receiving only maintenance from the citizens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Surrounding explanation: guardians are warrior-athletes who take care of the whole State; their households are common and individual possessions are abolished to prevent corruption. This institutional arrangement is presented as part of the 'perfect' city designed to produce the best citizens and rulers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosopher-kings' qualifications and end-goal
rubrics_metrics.description: True philosopher-kings must despise present-world honours, esteem above all things right and the honour that springs from right, regard justice as the greatest necessity, make philosophy their chief pursuit, and rule as a duty rather than for glory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance and consequences: such rulers are to be trained through a long program culminating in contemplation of the 'absolute good' and then to return to political life to order the State. They are to be honoured publicly (as demigods if the oracle consents) and to raise the city's principles according to the Form of the Good.

rubrics_metrics.name: State rearing and education policy
rubrics_metrics.description: The governors will send out all inhabitants over ten and take possession of their children, who are to be trained in the governors' habits and laws so that the State and constitution attain happiness more easily.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical procedure: children are removed from parental influence and educated in the laws and habits of the rulers. This is presented as the fastest route to instilling the right constitution in citizens; it underpins the communal-guardian system.

rubrics_metrics.name: Five constitutions taxonomy
rubrics_metrics.description: There are five principal forms of government (and corresponding human natures): aristocracy (the best), timocracy (honour-based), oligarchy (rule of the wealthy), democracy (rule by the many/lot), and tyranny (the worst disorder).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Context: Plato treats these as a progression from best to worst and as types that arise from human dispositions. He also notes hybrid and intermediate forms exist but focuses on these five distinct types for comparison and moral evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timocracy (government of honour) — origin and features
rubrics_metrics.description: Timocracy arises from aristocracy through mixture and the loss of some guardian virtues; it prizes honour, military training, common meals, and abstains from agriculture and trade. It has a spirit of contention and ambition and favors spirited/passionate characters suited to war rather than peace.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Features and dynamics: Timocratic regimes fear philosophers, emphasize gymnastics over music (culture), may wage continual wars, and harbor a secret longing for wealth despite ostensible disdain. The Muses' (mythic) account attributes its origin to mismanagement of births and the mingling of 'iron and brass' with 'gold and silver' natures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timocratic man (character corresponding to timocracy)
rubrics_metrics.description: The timocratic individual is contentious, ambitious, soldierly, prefers gymnastic and the chase, courteous to freemen but rough with slaves, a good listener but not a speaker, and becomes increasingly attracted to riches as he ages if philosophy is absent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Developmental account: such a man often has a brave but easy-going father and is driven by social complaints and examples to be more assertive; without philosophical tempering he gives the 'kingdom within' to the spirited element and becomes arrogant and ambitious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oligarchy (rule by property) — origin and defects
rubrics_metrics.description: Oligarchy is a government resting on a valuation of property: rulers are chosen by wealth qualification. Defects include a split between rich and poor (two states in one), incapacity or unwillingness to wage war effectively, extremes of wealth and poverty leading to paupers and criminal elements, and public officials chosen by property rather than merit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mechanics and pathologies: oligarchies legislate property-qualifications for citizenship, create social division and insecurity, encourage selfish accumulation, and produce social conditions (paupery, rogues) that undermine moral and civic health. Plato gives concrete examples: pilots chosen by wealth would shipwreck, and property-qualification makes the city fragile.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oligarchical man (character corresponding to oligarchy)
rubrics_metrics.description: The oligarchical individual values wealth above virtue, is penurious and laborious, confines desires to necessary appetites, often coerces bad passions by fear of loss rather than reason, and becomes 'two men' internally (better desires prevailing outwardly while base desires exist covertly).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Behavioral consequences: such men are respectable by appearance but lack unified soul harmony; they hoard wealth, avoid honorable contests that require spending, and show tendencies to dishonesty when entrusted with others' property (e.g., guardianship of an orphan).

rubrics_metrics.name: Democracy — origin and character
rubrics_metrics.description: Democracy arises when the poor conquer and are given equal freedom and power (magistrates often elected by lot). It is characterized by great freedom, frankness, a variety of human natures, equality of lifestyle choices, forgiving spirit, and a 'spangled' variety of manners—temporarily delightful but potentially disrespectful of earlier strict principles of civic education.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dynamics and judgment: Plato portrays democracy as attractive because of liberty and assortment of constitutions available, likening it to a market or embroidered robe. He also warns of its fragility: the same freedom that delights can lead to neglect of cultivation and to disorder; oligarchy's collapse into democracy is driven by wealth accumulation, debt, and class resentment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanisms of regime transition (causes of constitutional change)
rubrics_metrics.description: Constitutions change through human dispositions and social dynamics: divisions of governing power, fertility/sterility cycles, mismanagement of guardian selection/births, accumulation of private wealth, class resentment and revolt, and the interplay of honor, wealth, and freedom in successive generations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and causal chains: Plato sketches specific transitions—aristocracy → timocracy (mixture, loss of philosophical guardianship), timocracy → oligarchy (accumulation of private wealth), oligarchy → democracy (poverty, debt, and popular uprising), and implies further degeneration toward tyranny. He uses mythic numerical metaphors and social anecdotes to illustrate causes.
